name: Pelling, Yuksom & South Sikkim
meta_description: Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla and Namchi on a budget: Sikkim's first capitals, Pemayangtse, the Goecha La trail, homestays and shared jeep fares for 2025–26.
summary: West and South Sikkim hold the kingdom's oldest story: the 1642 crowning at Yuksom, the monasteries of Pemayangtse, Dubdi and Tashiding, the ruins of Rabdentse. Add Kanchenjunga dawns at Pelling, the Goecha La trail, Barsey's rhododendrons and village homestays, all reachable by shared jeep from Siliguri.

story.title: Three lamas, a stone throne and two lost capitals
paras: In 1642 three Tibetan lamas met in the forest at Yuksom: Lhatsun Chempo, Kathok Kuntu Zangpo and Ngadak Sempa Chempo. They had come over the mountains by different routes, and the local story says they were looking for a fourth man, from the east, to rule the hidden land that Guru Rinpoche had blessed centuries before. They found Phuntsog Namgyal and consecrated him as the first Chogyal of Sikkim at Norbugang. The stone throne, a chorten and an old pine still stand there, a short walk from Yuksom bazaar.

The kingdom's first monasteries grew around that moment. Tashiding was founded in 1641 by Ngadak Sempa Chempo and enlarged in 1717. Dubdi, above Yuksom, was built in 1701. Pemayangtse, founded around 1705 by Lhatsun Chempo's line, became the leading Nyingma monastery, whose head lama anointed the Chogyals. In 1670 the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved the capital to Rabdentse, on a ridge below Pelling. It held until Nepalese invasions in the late 18th century, and in 1814 the court moved to Tumlong in the north.

Long before the lamas, this was Lepcha country, and the Limboos farmed its western valleys. Lepcha tradition tells of Tendong Hill above Namchi rising to save their ancestors from a flood, and Sikkimese of every community honour Kanchenjunga as the land's guardian at Pang Lhabsol. Today the same hills grow large cardamom, oranges and Temi's tea, and the Kanchenjunga range is still the first thing people look at each morning.

intro: This land covers the western and southern districts of Sikkim: Gyalshing (the old West Sikkim district), Soreng, created in 2021, and Namchi (the old South Sikkim). Pelling is the base most people know, at about 2,150 m with the Kanchenjunga range across the valley. Beyond it the road runs to Yuksom, the first capital and the start of the Goecha La trail, and west to Dentam, Uttarey and Hee Bermiok, farming villages with homestays.

To the south, Ravangla and Namchi have Sikkim's large modern statues, the 130-foot Buddha at Tathagata Tsal and the 118-foot Guru Rinpoche on Samdruptse, along with Temi Tea Garden and quieter monasteries at Ralang and Kewzing. Rinchenpong and Kaluk, on the Soreng side, offer farm stays with mountain views, and the Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary lies along the Singalila ridge above them.

It is good value country. Shared jeeps link Siliguri, Jorethang, Gyalshing and the villages; homestays include dinner and breakfast; most monasteries charge little or nothing. The catch is time: jeeps leave in the morning, roads are winding and the monsoon brings landslides. Plan fewer bases and longer stays, and you will spend less and see more.

highlights.title: Yuksom and the coronation throne
highlights.text: Sikkim's first capital, where three lamas consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal in 1642. Walk to the stone throne at Norbugang, Kathok Lake and Dubdi Monastery, built in 1701, then watch trekkers set off for Goecha La from the same village.

highlights.title: Pemayangtse and Rabdentse
highlights.text: The leading Nyingma monastery of Sikkim, founded around 1705, with a seven-tiered wooden palace on its top floor, and a forest walk away, the ruins of Rabdentse, capital from 1670. Both are an easy walk from Upper Pelling.

highlights.title: Kanchenjunga from Pelling
highlights.text: From Upper Pelling the Kanchenjunga range fills the northern sky on clear mornings, most reliably from October to December and in March and April. Stay two dawns rather than one, and go up to the rooftop before 6 am.

highlights.title: The Goecha La and Dzongri trails
highlights.text: Trek from Yuksom into Khangchendzonga National Park, a UNESCO mixed World Heritage Site since 2016, to Dzongri Top at about 4,000 m or View Point 1 below Goecha La at about 4,600 m. Guides and permits are mandatory.

highlights.title: Tashiding and Khecheopalri
highlights.text: Two of the holiest places in Sikkim: a hilltop monastery founded in 1641, where the Bumchu vase is opened each spring, and a quiet lake sacred to Buddhists and Hindus, its surface said to be kept clear of leaves by birds.

highlights.title: Ravangla, Namchi and Temi
highlights.text: South Sikkim's statues of the Buddha and Guru Rinpoche, the Char Dham complex at Solophok, the Lepcha story of Tendong Hill and Temi Tea Garden, set up in 1969. Short drives, frequent jeeps and an easy family trip.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), both on the edge of Siliguri. For Pelling, take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Jorethang (about ₹250–350 a seat) and change for Pelling or Gyalshing (₹150–220); a few direct jeeps to Pelling leave in the morning at ₹450–600. For Ravangla and Namchi, direct shared jeeps from Siliguri cost about ₹250–400. Jorethang is the hub for Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Hee Bermiok and Uttarey; Gyalshing for Yuksom and Tashiding. A reserved small car from NJP costs about ₹5,000–6,500 to Pelling and ₹4,500–5,500 to Ravangla (indicative). From Gangtok, jeeps run to Ravangla, Namchi and Gyalshing; from Darjeeling, go via Jorethang. Jeeps leave mostly in the morning: start early.
permits: Indian citizens need no permit for Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla, Namchi and the villages of this land; carry photo ID for checkposts. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which can be applied for online and is checked at entry points such as Rangpo and Melli. Treks to Dzongri and Goecha La need a Khangchendzonga National Park permit issued at Yuksom, police registration and a licensed guide; foreign trekkers must go through a registered agency. Sanctuaries such as Barsey charge entry fees. Rules and fees change: check current status before you travel.
money: A shoestring day here costs about ₹1,800–2,500 per person: a shared jeep seat, a homestay with dinner and breakfast at ₹1,500–2,200, a bazaar lunch of momos or a thali and a monastery donation. A comfortable day, with a reserved car shared by two and a mountain-view room, costs ₹4,000–6,500. Treks are priced separately, roughly ₹3,000–4,000 a day on the trail with a local agency. People overspend on reserved cars for short hops that jeeps cover, on single-night stays that waste half a day moving, and on Pelling hotels in October and Puja weeks, when rates can double. Carry cash: ATMs are few outside Gyalshing, Jorethang, Namchi and Ravangla.

months.weather: Pelling about 0–10 °C, dry, clear mornings, frost
months.summary: The coldest month and one of the clearest. Kanchenjunga is often visible all morning from Pelling, Rinchenpong and Ravangla, rooms are cheap and the roads are quiet. Nights fall close to freezing at 2,000 m, and budget rooms rarely have heating, so pack properly. High treks above Tshoka are snowbound and not advisable. A good month for monasteries and slow village stays at lower altitude.
months.tip: Ask for a room with a heater or extra quilts and confirm hot water timings before you check in.

months.weather: Pelling about 2–12 °C, mostly dry, occasional snow on ridges
months.summary: Still cold, still clear, with the first warmth in the afternoons. The Pemayangtse cham and Losar usually fall in February or early March, and Bumchu at Tashiding follows about two weeks after Losar. Rooms near Tashiding fill at festival time; elsewhere it is low season. Treks are still closed by snow above Dzongri in most years.
months.tip: Check the lunar calendar dates for the cham and Bumchu before booking, as they move every year.

months.weather: Pelling about 5–16 °C, mostly dry, afternoon haze building
months.summary: Spring begins. Rhododendrons start flowering at Barsey and on the forest trails, magnolias bloom around Ravangla and the first flush is picked at Temi. Mornings are still clear for Kanchenjunga, with more haze by afternoon. Bumchu can fall in March. Late March is a good time to start the Dzongri trek if snow allows.
months.tip: Plan Barsey for late March or April and ask in Hilley how far the bloom has climbed.

months.weather: Pelling about 8–19 °C, warm days, some afternoon showers
months.summary: Peak rhododendron season at Barsey and along the Goecha La trail, and the start of the main spring trekking season from Yuksom. Views are good early in the morning and often lost to cloud by noon. School holidays and long weekends bring crowds to Pelling and Ravangla, so book ahead.
months.tip: Be on your viewpoint by 5.30 am; April views rarely last past 9 am.

months.weather: Pelling about 11–21 °C, warmer, more frequent showers
months.summary: The last good trekking month before the monsoon, with rhododendrons still in flower higher up and green valleys below. Pelling and Ravangla are busy with summer holidaymakers from the plains. Showers become more frequent towards the end of the month, and views are less reliable than in April.
months.tip: Finish any high trek by the third week of May, before pre-monsoon storms set in.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives. Rain, mist and leeches cover the hills, treks close, and landslides start to block roads, sometimes for hours, sometimes for days. Prices fall sharply. If you come, choose one base with good road access such as Namchi or Ravangla and keep buffer days.
months.tip: Travel in the morning, when rain is usually lighter, and never schedule a train or flight on the day you come down.

months.weather: Pelling about 15–21 °C, heavy rain most days
months.summary: The wettest stretch of the year. Waterfalls on the Yuksom road are at their fullest, the tea at Temi is lush and the valleys very green, but views are rare and roads unpredictable. Only for patient travellers with flexible plans and a taste for misty forest.
months.tip: Carry salt or leech socks for any forest walk and check road status each morning.

months.summary: Still the monsoon. Tendong Lho Rum Faat on 8 August is the main event, celebrated by Lepcha communities across Sikkim with special meaning near Namchi. Pang Lhabsol may fall at the end of August. Expect road delays and plan buffer days.
months.tip: Base yourself in Namchi or Ravangla, which have better road links than the western villages.

months.weather: Pelling about 13–20 °C, rain easing late in the month
months.summary: The monsoon fades, usually in the second half of the month. Pang Lhabsol often falls in September, with warrior dances at Ravangla. The hills are green and the first clear mornings return, though landslide repairs may still be under way. Prices stay low until the Puja holidays begin.
months.tip: Book Puja-week rooms in September if your holiday falls in early October.

months.summary: The best month for views and the start of the autumn trekking season from Yuksom. Durga Puja and Diwali bring large crowds from Bengal and beyond, and Pelling hotel prices can double in those weeks. Outside the holidays, it is close to perfect: clear mornings, mild days and dry trails.
months.tip: Avoid the Puja week in Pelling if you can, or book a village homestay instead.

months.summary: Often the clearest month of the year. Kanchenjunga stands out all morning, the Goecha La trail is busy until mid-month and the villages are harvesting rice and drying cardamom. Nights turn cold. Prices ease after Diwali, making late November a very good value time.
months.tip: Trek in the first half of the month; after that, Dzongri and above get very cold.

months.summary: Cold, clear and quiet until the Christmas and New Year rush. Kanchenjunga views are reliable, rooms are cheaper before 20 December and village homestays are warm with kitchen fires. High treks are mostly over; snow arrives above Dzongri. A good month for budget honeymoons and long weekends.
months.tip: Book Christmas week early in Pelling, or stay in Rinchenpong, which stays quieter.

faqs.q: What is the best base for West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Pelling, for most first-time visitors. It has the widest choice of budget rooms, the most jeeps and the easiest walks to Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sanga Choeling, plus Kanchenjunga views. Add Yuksom for history and treks, and a village such as Uttarey, Kaluk or Hee Bermiok for quiet.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Pelling, Yuksom and South Sikkim?
faqs.a: At least five nights for Pelling and Yuksom alone, eight to nine nights to add Ravangla, Namchi and a village stay, and nine to ten nights for the Goecha La trek. Shared jeeps run mostly in the morning, so each move costs half a day.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Pelling and Yuksom?
faqs.a: No. Indian citizens need only photo ID for Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla, Namchi and the villages. Treks into Khangchendzonga National Park, such as Dzongri and Goecha La, need a park permit, police registration and a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get from Siliguri to Pelling cheaply?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Jorethang, about ₹250–350, and change for Pelling or Gyalshing, about ₹150–220. A few direct jeeps run in the morning at ₹450–600. Leave Siliguri by 10 am. A reserved small car costs about ₹5,000–6,500 (indicative).

faqs.q: Where can I see Kanchenjunga in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: From Upper Pelling, Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Hee Bermiok, Ravangla and the Barsey ridge, and at close range from Dzongri and Goecha La View Point 1. Clear mornings are most reliable from October to December and in March and April. Be out before sunrise.

faqs.q: What is the history of Yuksom?
faqs.a: Yuksom was Sikkim's first capital. In 1642 three Tibetan lamas consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal at Norbugang, where a stone throne still stands. The name is usually explained as the meeting place of the three lamas. Dubdi Monastery above the village dates from 1701.

faqs.q: Is West Sikkim good for a budget trip?
faqs.a: Yes. Shared jeeps, village homestays with meals at ₹1,500–2,200 per person and free or low-cost monasteries keep a shoestring day to about ₹1,800–2,500. The main costs to watch are reserved cars and peak-season hotels in Pelling during Durga Puja and Diwali.

faqs.q: When are the roads in West Sikkim affected by landslides?
faqs.a: Mostly from June to September, during the monsoon, when slides can close roads for hours or days. The Melli–Jorethang and Legship–Pelling roads and the village roads beyond Pelling are often affected. Keep buffer days and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Pelling and Yuksom?
faqs.a: Yes, with a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which can be applied for online and is checked at entry points such as Rangpo and Melli. Foreign trekkers going to Dzongri or Goecha La must also travel with a registered agency, usually in a group. Check current status before you travel.
